title: Purim: hearing Esther
hook: the whole scroll read, with noise at Haman's name
tomorrow: why does Purim send you to two poor people?

segments.voice: Yesterday, Tu BiShvat: Honi's carob, planted for grandchildren the planter would never meet. Plant something. Now a scroll, and a room full of noisemakers.
screen: `PLANT SOMETHING.` → `A SCROLL AND A ROOM FULL OF NOISE.`

segments.voice: Skipping an episode can wreck a whole series. On Purim, the Book of Esther is read from a scroll, the Megillah, and the rule is to hear every word. When the villain Haman's name comes up, the room erupts, rattles, stamping, booing, to blot it out. Then silence, so the next words can be heard. And the scroll has a strange feature for a book of the Bible. In the Hebrew, God is never named.
screen: `DON'T SKIP AN EPISODE.` → `NOISE FOR HAMAN, THEN SILENCE.` → `GOD IS NEVER NAMED.`

segments.voice: So today's question: can God be in a story that never says God's name? The rabbis answer with a play on Esther's name. They hear in it the Hebrew of a line from Deuteronomy: "I will surely hide My face." A hidden God, working through palace gossip, a sleepless king, a dinner at the right moment. That's why the reading has a rule. The Mishnah says that if you read the scroll out of order, you haven't done it. Every word, in sequence, because the hand only shows in the whole chain. That's why the noise stops. Christians read this scroll too. In the King James Bible, Mordecai's question to Esther runs: "and who knoweth whether thou art come to the kingdom for such a time as this?" The shared ground is real: a young woman who risks the palace to save her people, and a question about why you're standing where you are. And an honest difference. Catholic and Orthodox Bibles include extra chapters from the Greek, in which Mordecai and Esther pray aloud and God is named. Protestant Bibles set those chapters apart, among the Apocrypha. The Hebrew scroll keeps its silence. The same story, heard two ways, and each tradition keeps its own.
screen: `ESTHER, AND "I WILL SURELY HIDE."` · `OUT OF ORDER DOESN'T COUNT.` · `"FOR SUCH A TIME AS THIS."` · `THE GREEK CHAPTERS NAME GOD.` · then, large: `HEAR IT ALL.`

segments.voice: For the sit, listen to your breath as a story told in order: the start of the inhale, its middle, the turn, the long way out. Don't skip ahead to the end of any breath. If a noise interrupts, let it, then come back for the next word, the way the room goes quiet after Haman.
screen: `A BREATH, IN ORDER.` · `DON'T SKIP AHEAD.` · `BACK FOR THE NEXT WORD.`

segments.voice: Purim: lots. Haman "cast pur, that is, the lot," to pick a day; the festival is named for it, and the whole scroll is heard.
Hold on to this: hear it all. Every word, in order, even the quiet ones where God is hiding.

howItsDone: On Purim, Jews hear the Megillah, the scroll of Esther, read aloud in the evening and again in the morning, following along word by word and making noise with groggers or stamping at Haman's name.

notes: Deuteronomy 31:18 and Esther 3:7 JPS 1917: confirm exact wording. Esther 4:14 is quoted from the KJV on purpose, as the Christian Bible's wording (unity thread).
Chullin 139b ('Esther from the Torah: haster astir'): a rabbinic wordplay, not an etymology. Confirm phrasing.
'In the Hebrew, God is never named' in Esther: confirm (the divine name does not appear in the Masoretic text).

Additions to Esther: in Catholic and Orthodox Bibles (Douay-Rheims chapters 10:4–16:24, prayers in 13–14); Protestant Bibles place them in the Apocrypha or omit them. 'Set apart, among the Apocrypha' simplifies; confirm a Christian reader would find it fair.
Unity thread (wisdom day): shared ground (the same scroll and Mordecai's question) plus one honest difference (Greek chapters naming God vs the Hebrew scroll's silence), ranking none.
Parents: the Esther story includes Haman's plan to destroy the Jews and later violence (ch. 9); the lesson names Haman only as 'the villain' and keeps details out.
Fork answer simplified to 'catch up on what you missed' (halakha: one who missed words should hear or read them, e.g. from a printed text, in order). Confirm.
